name: Erik Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the hired man on the Haas farm, sixty milking cows and about ninety hectares of barley and grass. Alarm goes at half four, I'm in the parlour by five, and milking takes me nearly two hours because it's an old herringbone setup with eight stalls a side. Then it's scraping out, feeding, checking the young stock, and in summer I'm on the tractor till dark. I like the cows, honestly, they each have a temper you get to know.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The hours, and the pay for the hours. Walter and Ingrid are decent people, but the dairy pays them next to nothing for milk, so they pay me next to nothing too. I live in the little cottage on the farm with my girlfriend Lena, she does shifts at the care home in town. The cottage comes with the job, so if I lose the job, we lose the roof too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hype. Yes, that sounds about right to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say told you so, mostly. There's a lad at the feed merchant, Dominik, who keeps showing me videos of robot arms milking cows, and I'd send him one back saying where's my robot then. Online I don't post much, but I'd probably share something about how the money went to tech firms instead of to farmers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my life stays the same, and my life is hard but I know it. I'd still be up at half four, still paid badly, still in the cottage. The milk price would still be the thing that decides whether Walter keeps me on, not some computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing new, really. I'd keep going with the milking and the barley, try to get Walter to fix the parlour pump before winter, and maybe push again for a small raise in spring. I wouldn't touch any of the AI apps, I don't use them now and I wouldn't start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relief, mostly. Like a storm forecast that passes to the north of you and you still have to fix the fence anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the money went to tech firms instead of farmers. Who do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big processors and the people selling the gadgets. The dairy that collects our milk had a new app last year to track quality, and nobody asked whether the farmers wanted it, they just charged a fee for it. If all that money had gone into the milk price instead, Walter could pay me properly and fix the roof on the calf shed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing changes, what does the next year look like for you and Lena?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About the same, which is fine and not fine. We've got maybe three weeks of money put aside, and that's after a good month. We'd like to save for a deposit on a place of our own one day, but at this rate it's a long way off.

S0.say: It was hype all along, and the money that went into it should have gone to farmers and workers instead. I'd joke about it with the lads at the feed merchant who kept showing me robot videos.
S0.think: My life would stay the same, which means hard but familiar. The milk price, not technology, would still decide whether I keep my job and the cottage that comes with it.
S0.do: Carries on milking and working the barley as before. Pushes the farmer to repair the parlour pump and asks again for a small raise in spring. Keeps avoiding AI apps.
S0.feel: Relieved, the way you are when a storm passes to the north. Still tired of low pay.
S0.quote: If all that money had gone into the milk price instead, Walter could pay me properly and fix the roof on the calf shed.
S0.fieldNote: Erik is calm here because his worries are about milk prices and pay, not technology. His tied cottage came up in the opening and frames everything: job and home are the same thing. He already blames processors and tech sellers for squeezing farmers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Many tasks in many jobs. Milking is a task, isn't it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules, and we need farmworkers in the room when the rules get written. At the pub I'd say the same thing I say about everything: if the machine makes money, the people it replaces should get a share. I'd probably finally join the farmworkers' section of the union, I've been meaning to for two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think Walter would buy a milking robot the minute the bank lent him the money. He's sixty-three and his knees are gone, and a robot doesn't ask for a raise. He'd feel bad about it, he'd buy me a drink, and I'd be out of a job and a house by the next spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the union this winter, properly, pay the dues. I'd ask Walter straight out what his plans are for the parlour so I'm not caught by surprise. Beyond that I'd wait and see, because I don't know what else I'd train for round here, and I'm not going to start playing with apps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like hearing a noise in the barn at night and not wanting to go and look.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't start with the apps. Some people in your spot would learn to run the robot. Why not you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the robot doesn't need running, that's the whole point of it. Someone from the dealer comes out when it breaks, and that's a job for a lad with a laptop in the city, not me. Maybe I'm being stubborn, Lena says I am, but I'd rather spend my time on the cows than on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Walter did buy one, where would you look for work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the problem. There are maybe four dairy farms within thirty kilometres and two have already got robots. I'd probably end up driving for the grain co-op at harvest and whatever else I could get in winter, and we'd have to find a flat in town on Lena's wage.

S1.say: We need rules on this and farmworkers need a say in them. If a machine makes money by replacing people, those people should get a share. I'd finally join the union.
S1.think: The farmer would likely buy a milking robot as soon as the bank allowed it, and I'd lose my job and the cottage with it. There are few dairy jobs left nearby.
S1.do: Joins the farmworkers' section of the union this winter and pays the dues. Asks the farmer directly about his plans for the parlour. Otherwise waits to see what happens rather than retraining or learning new tools.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a noise in the barn at night that he doesn't want to check.
S1.quote: He'd feel bad about it, he'd buy me a drink, and I'd be out of a job and a house by the next spring.
S1.fieldNote: The tied cottage turns any job threat into a housing threat, and he knows it. He reaches for the union rather than new skills, and openly admits Lena calls him stubborn. He's not angry at his boss, he expects the boss to feel guilty and do it anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's two more calving seasons. That's nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be loud about it, for once. I'd say the government has to stop it or slow it down, and anyone whose work gets taken should get paid while they sort themselves out. I'd sign every petition going and I'd go to the protest in the city if the union organised one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be finished in farming. If a robot can milk, drive and fix a fence, Walter has no reason to keep me, and nobody else round here will hire me either. I've got a vocational certificate in agriculture and three weeks of savings, and neither of those is worth much when the machine does it cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, we'd stop spending on anything we don't need, no takeaways, no trip to Lena's sister in the summer. I'd go to the council and find out what housing help there is before we need it, not after. I'd do the union stuff, the petitions, the votes, and I'd ask my parents if we could stay with them for a bit if it came to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked, if I'm honest. My chest goes tight just saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lena that first night, when you knew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say nothing for an hour and then say sorry. She'd tell me it's not my fault, and she'd be right, but I'd still feel it was. I'd say we might be sleeping in my old bedroom at my mum's, and I'm twenty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you wouldn't learn the new tools. With only two years, does that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, because two years isn't long enough to learn anything that a machine won't already do better. That's what scares me. With the slow version I could pretend there'd be some corner left for me, but in this one there isn't a corner.

S2.say: The government has to slow this down, and anyone whose work is taken should be paid while they find their feet. I'd sign every petition and turn up to any union protest.
S2.think: I'd be finished in farming, with no reason for the farmer to keep me and no one else hiring nearby. Three weeks of savings and a vocational certificate won't protect me.
S2.do: Cuts all spare spending straight away, including a summer trip. Visits the council to ask about housing help before he needs it and asks his parents about moving in. Signs petitions and joins union protests.
S2.feel: Panicked, with a tight chest. Guilty towards his girlfriend, even though he knows it isn't his fault.
S2.quote: I'd say we might be sleeping in my old bedroom at my mum's, and I'm twenty-seven.
S2.fieldNote: This is the scenario that breaks him: job, home and skills all go at once with almost no savings. He refuses to learn new tools even here, but his reason shifts from stubbornness to a belief that there's no corner left to learn into. The image of moving back to his childhood bedroom carries real shame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay. That's a bit different, but not much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, but I'd say it louder and earlier, because there'd be time for it to matter. I'd want the union to push for a law that says a farm can't evict a worker from a tied cottage just because a robot came in. I'd be in the meetings, I'd be the one handing out leaflets at the market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years just means I see it coming longer. I'd still be thirty-two with nothing much behind me. The difference is I'd have time to put a bit aside, and time to be scared for longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to save properly, maybe a hundred a month, which sounds small but it's more than we save now. I'd stay with Walter as long as he'd keep me, and I'd spend the time on the union and on getting the cottage rules changed. Learning to code or whatever, no, that's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Not as tight as the two-year one, but it'd keep me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd save a hundred a month. Where does that come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena and I would sell the second car, the old hatchback, and share hers. I'd stop buying cigarettes, which I should do anyway. That's most of a hundred right there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the extra three years change for you, compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They give me a chance to fight it instead of just taking it. In two years there's no time to change any law, but in five you could get something through, maybe. It doesn't change what happens to my job, it changes whether I go down without saying anything.

S3.say: With five years there's time to fight for proper rules, like protecting farmworkers in tied cottages. I'd be at the union meetings and handing out leaflets.
S3.think: Five years mostly means seeing it coming for longer. I'd be thirty-two with little behind me, but I'd have time to save a little and to push for change.
S3.do: Sells the second car and quits smoking to save about a hundred a month. Stays with the farmer as long as possible. Spends his time on union campaigning for rules on tied housing.
S3.feel: Alarmed and losing sleep, though less than in the two-year picture.
S3.quote: The difference is I'd have time to put a bit aside, and time to be scared for longer.
S3.fieldNote: For Erik, the extra time is about politics, not career change. He sees the five years as a window to change rules on tied housing rather than to retrain. He's honest that he still won't learn new tech. The second car and cigarettes were concrete and very quick to come up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. Walter would be retired by then anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got ten years to make sure this goes to everyone and not just the people who own the machines. I'd want public money for farmworkers to retrain, and I'd say that at every union meeting. Online I'd share the union stuff, same as before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think ten years means I'd probably be gone from the Haas farm before the robots even matter, because Walter will retire and sell up. Whoever buys it will be a big outfit, and big outfits buy robots. So the end is the same, it's just further away, and I'd be tempted to keep my head down and hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep saving, the hundred a month, and maybe more if I got a raise. I'd keep up the union work and vote for whoever promises proper support for people pushed out of work. I'd probably wait a few years to see how real it looks before doing anything drastic like moving or retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. More like a weight than a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you did have to retrain in the end, what would you even want to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've thought about it, actually. Maybe something with animals that people still want a person for, like working at the vet's or a farm park where kids come. People will still want to see a human holding a lamb, I reckon, even if a robot fed it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep your head down and hope. Does ten years make that easier or harder?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Easier, which is the trouble. Ten years is long enough that I'd tell myself I've got time, and then I'd be thirty-five and still milking. Lena would kick me, though. She's the one who makes the plans, I'm the one who milks the cows.

S4.say: We have ten years to make sure the gains go to everyone, not just the people who own the machines. I'd push for public money to help farmworkers retrain.
S4.think: The farmer will likely retire and sell to a big outfit before then, and they'll bring robots. Ten years makes it easy to keep my head down and hope, which is a trap.
S4.do: Keeps saving about a hundred a month. Stays active in the union and votes for parties promising support for displaced workers. Waits a few years before deciding on any move or retraining.
S4.feel: Anxious, like a weight rather than a panic. Some hope that people will still want a human with the animals.
S4.quote: People will still want to see a human holding a lamb, I reckon, even if a robot fed it.
S4.fieldNote: Erik knows ten years could lull him, and says so himself. His only retraining idea keeps him close to animals and people, not machines. He relies heavily on his girlfriend as the planner in the couple. The end point still frightens him, but the decade takes the edge off.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, by a mile. That's the one where we lose the job and the cottage in the same month and I've got no time to do anything. What would help is if a farm couldn't put a worker out of a tied house for a year after a robot comes in, and some money to live on while we found our feet.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who owns the robots. Nobody ever asks that. If the farmers owned them, or a co-op did, it might be different, but it'll be the dealer and the bank. I'd like someone to write that down.

headlineQuote: She's the one who makes the plans, I'm the one who milks the cows.
portrait: Erik Bauer is a 27-year-old hired hand on a sixty-cow dairy and barley farm, living with his girlfriend Lena in a cottage that comes with the job. He has about three weeks of savings, a vocational certificate and little interest in new technology, which he never uses. He's pro-union and blames processors and tech sellers for squeezing farmers. He stays calm if AI stalls, grows uneasy at steady change, and panics at AGI in two years because he'd lose his job and home together. With more warning he turns to union campaigning and small savings, not retraining, and admits a decade might tempt him to keep his head down.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he'd lose his job and the cottage that comes with it in the same month, with no time to act.
whatWouldHelp: He wants a rule that farms can't evict workers from tied housing for a year after bringing in robots, plus money to live on while people find their feet.
